entities.summary:
Cao Zhi (192–232 CE) was a pivotal figure in the development of Chinese poetry during the tumultuous Three Kingdoms period, specifically within the state of Cao Wei. As the third son of the powerful warlord Cao Cao and a younger brother to the future Emperor Wen, Cao Pi, his literary genius, characterized by a poignant blend of emotional depth and elegant form, profoundly influenced the Jian'an style. His work provides an invaluable window into the intellectual and cultural ferment of an age defined by political fragmentation and artistic innovation, establishing him as one of the "Three Caos" alongside his father and brother, who collectively shaped the trajectory of Chinese literary tradition for centuries.

Despite his considerable poetic talent, Cao Zhi's life was largely overshadowed by political intrigue and his elder brother Cao Pi's ascension to power. During his father Cao Cao's lifetime, Cao Zhi was often favored for his literary brilliance and intellectual prowess, leading to a period of intense rivalry with Cao Pi for succession. Following Cao Pi's usurpation of the Han dynasty and establishment of the Cao Wei state in 220 CE, Cao Zhi was systematically marginalized and subjected to strict surveillance, frequently moved between different fiefdoms. His most celebrated works, such as the 'Ode to the Goddess of the Luo River' (Luòshén Fù) and numerous 'shi' poems, reflect his personal frustrations, melancholic reflections on transient glory, and a profound appreciation for natural beauty, often employing vivid imagery and sophisticated rhetorical devices.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Cao Zhi's mastery of the five-character-line verse and his emphasis on personal expression fundamentally reshaped Chinese poetry, setting a foundational aesthetic for subsequent dynastic periods and influencing major poets for centuries. He is considered one of the 'Three Caos,' whose collective literary output defined the Jian'an style.
